items.title: 14.10.1 Main health risks associated with air pollution

source_refs.note: Topic 14.10.1 as printed, with Quick Check 14.4 printed at its end, printed pages 315-316.

blocks.text: Air pollutants such as ozone, particular matters (PM) and nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) can increase asthma symptoms and trigger asthma attack. Long term exposure may lead to chronic cough and respiratory infections like pneumonia.
Exposure to particular matters and other pollutants can increase the risk of heart attack by causing inflammation, blood vessel damage, high blood pressure and finally heart stroke.
Prolonged exposure to certain air pollutants especially particulate matter (PM) and carcinogenic compounds (benzene formation) cause lung cancer.
Exposure to air pollution may negatively impact reproductive health and fertility in both man and women. Premature birth and developmental problems in children may occur.

blocks.prompt: a) Explain the impact of particulate matter (PM) on the air quality.
blocks.explanation: Particles suspended in the air make it hazy and raise the AQI. When breathed in, they cause inflammation and irritation of the airways, leading to asthma and bronchitis; fine PM2.5 reaches deep into the lungs and also raises the risk of heart disease and lung cancer.

blocks.prompt: b) What is AQI? How does it measure air quality?
blocks.explanation: AQI (Air Quality Index) is a measure of the concentration of pollutants (PM, NO₂, SO₂, CO, O₃) in the air at a particular place. The measured concentrations are converted into a single number from 0 to 500; the higher the number, the poorer the air.

blocks.prompt: c) What are different levels of AQI. Mention the safest and the most hazardous ranges of AQI.
blocks.explanation: Good 0–50 (green), moderate 51–100 (yellow), unhealthy for sensitive groups 101–150 (orange), unhealthy 151–200 (red), very unhealthy 201–300 (purple) and hazardous 301–500 (maroon). The safest range is 0–50 and the most hazardous is 301–500.
